title: Disciplinary Knowledge in English
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart applies his four-rung progression of conceptual development (substantive knowledge, substantive concepts, disciplinary knowledge, disciplinary concepts) to English, a subject he says fits neither the enquiry question 'How do we know?' nor the practice question 'What does good look like and why?' because literacy is both medium and object. He argues that primary English commonly repeats the 'think like an expert' mistake by starting with the features of a text type or the labels of grammar, which are the expert's end point, rather than building the knowledge those features depend on. A pupil can tick every feature and still write a letter that persuades no one, and a word has no class until it is doing a job in context. In his model, disciplinary knowledge in English is effect on the reader, with disciplinary concepts such as suspense, tone and sympathy naming those effects. He shows how the same ladder works in secondary using Of Mice and Men and warns that planning only from the mark scheme brings the features checklist back, concluding that features, grammar terms and specifications belong later in the progression in service of effect.
points: Because language is both the medium and the object in English, no single guiding question runs through the whole subject, which is why its progression is hard to see.
Teaching text-type features or grammar labels first hands pupils the expert's end point and skips the substantive knowledge that makes those features meaningful.
Disciplinary knowledge in English is essentially effect on the reader, and for a writer it is what good looks like for this reader and purpose.
Oral work lets young pupils access effect early, since a child still learning to write can hear that a story is tense and say why.
In secondary, choose context only as far as comprehension of the text needs it, and avoid planning solely from the mark scheme.
quotes: The expert’s end point, in the form of text features, word classes or exam specifications, can look like the subject itself.
In science, pupils use language to learn about the world. In English, they use language to learn about language.
A list of text features, even annotated on a new text, says nothing about why it works. A child can include every feature and still write a letter that persuades no one.
The class is decided by context so it is an outcome of understanding. Starting with the class turns the order round.
Children can sort words and phrases into columns and still not use the knowledge when they write because the task is removed from actual communication.
The discipline of English is dependent on knowledge, not written fluency, so a child still learning to read and write can hear that a story is tense and say why.
The mistake is treating any of them as the starting point. They belong on the progression after the cases and in service of effect.
